name: Fatima Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for seeing me, Fatima. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. What you say is confidential. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My husband Declan and I own Hillcrest, a mixed farm with 12,000 free-range laying hens and 200 hectares of wheat and oilseed rape. I run the hens and the egg side, Declan runs the arable and the machines. I'm in the hen houses at seven checking water lines and the birds' behaviour, and the eggs go to Greenvale, the packing company we've supplied for fifteen years.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the hens, honestly. You walk in and you can tell in ten seconds if the flock is happy. What wears me out is bird flu season, when we have to keep them shut in for months, and the yearly contract talks with Greenvale, which get harder every time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's a picture I can believe. We use a couple of apps already and they're handy, not magic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at the farmers' discussion group that it's what most of us expected: a few useful tools and a lot of noise. I'm not one for big statements online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my worries stay where they are. Bird flu, feed prices and the Greenvale contract are what keep me up, and AI doesn't change any of them. We're comfortable, but egg farming always feels one bad season from trouble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with the same flock and the same contract. I'd keep using the app that tracks egg numbers and feed, which I picked up last year after the neighbours did. And we'd keep building the savings for a bad bird flu year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady, but never fully relaxed. That's eggs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said one bad season from trouble. With strong savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The savings would carry us through one bad year, not two. We could survive one bird flu year at Hillcrest (her family farm), but two in a row would eat everything Declan (her husband) and I have saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you talk to about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Declan, over supper, and our son Ciarán, who wants to take over the hens. He's 29 and keen. I'd want him to know the risks.

I'd keep it to the **discussion group**, not online.
think: **Bird flu**, feed prices and the Greenvale contract still worry me.
Egg farming always feels **one bad season** from trouble.
do: Keep the **same flock** and Greenvale contract.
Keep using the **egg-tracking app** I picked up last year.
Keep building **savings** for a bad bird flu year.
feel: She feels **steady**, but never fully relaxed.

fieldNote: Her unease comes from **existing pressures**: bird flu and the packer contract.

steps.text: Keep the 12,000 hens on the same Greenvale contract
Keep using the egg and feed tracking app
Keep building savings for a bad bird flu year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office side going to computers. That would hit Greenvale before it hits my hens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at the discussion group that farmers need to understand the new contracts, because the packers will use AI to squeeze us. I'd want the farmers' union to look at it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think Greenvale would use AI to set prices and grade eggs tighter. The hen work stays mine, but the money side gets harder. Maybe a tenth less on the egg price over a few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the farm business course the union runs, once a few others have done it, so I can read what the AI contracts mean. I'd let Ciarán take on the record-keeping software. And we'd look at selling some eggs direct, through a vending machine at the farm gate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like walking into a contract meeting with the other side holding better cards.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the vending machine?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Greenvale's (the egg packer's) computer squeezes the egg price, a vending machine at the farm gate is my way of not putting all my eggs in one basket. Sorry, I had to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Declan think?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say the arable is fine, wheat's wheat. He'd be right, but the hens are half our income.

say: I'd say farmers must **understand the new contracts**.
I'd want the **farmers' union** to look at AI pricing.
think: Greenvale would use AI to **squeeze prices** and grading.
We might lose **a tenth** on the egg price over a few years.
do: Take the union's **farm business course** after others try it.
Let **Ciarán** take on the record software.
Put an **egg vending machine** at the farm gate.
feel: She feels **uneasy**, like the other side holds better cards.

fieldNote: She sees AI arriving through the **buyer's side**, not her own sheds.
Her answer is to **diversify sales** with a farm-gate machine.
She hands the **software** to her son rather than learning it all herself.

steps.text: Take the farmers' union business course once others have
Put an egg vending machine at the farm gate

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years for the thinking, five for robots. I'd be 63 and Ciarán 34. That's a lot at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government needs to protect family farms from the giants who can buy robots first. I'd say it at the union and I'd vote for whoever promised that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the huge egg units would go fully robotic in 2031 and undercut us. Greenvale would pick their cheapest supplier, and that wouldn't be us. Our hen income could halve, and Ciarán's future with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with Declan and Ciarán this winter and decide whether to invest in robots in 2030 or get out of eggs. I'd put money aside for the first option, maybe 80,000. And I'd keep the arable going as our safe half.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I can feel it in my chest just thinking about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Ciarán?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my son Ciarán that the hens might not be a living by the time he's thirty-five, and I'd hate saying it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd consider robots yourself. Would you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the neighbours did and it worked, yes. I'm not first, but I'm not last either. I'd rather own the robot than compete with it.

I'd **vote** for whoever promised that, and say so at the union.
think: Robotic egg units in **2031** would undercut Hillcrest.
Our **hen income could halve**, and Ciarán's future with it.
do: Decide with Declan and Ciarán: **robots or out** of eggs.
Set aside about **80,000** for robots in 2030.
Keep the **arable** as our safe half.
feel: She feels **anxious**, a tightness in her chest.
S2.quote: I'd tell my son Ciarán that the hens might not be a living by the time he's thirty-five, and I'd hate saying it.
fieldNote: Her hands-on work lasts until **2031**, but the buyer's AI hits pricing in **2028**.
She fears **half the household income** going if eggs fail.
Her **son's future** is the sharpest part of the worry.

steps.text: Decide with her husband and son between egg robots or leaving eggs
Set aside about 80,000 to buy robots in 2030
Vote for protections for family farms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, robots in 2034. I'd be 66 and Ciarán would have time to learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've been given a fair warning, and farming groups should use it to buy together. I'd push the union to set up a shared buying group for the new kit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be stepping back by 2034 anyway. It's really Ciarán's decision, and five years gives him time to learn and decide. I'd feel better about this one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd send Ciarán on the robot and AI courses as they come out, and let him run trials once the neighbours have shown they work. I'd keep saving for the kit. And I'd plan to hand over the hens to him at 65.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more hopeful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would change for you personally?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much day to day. The hens would still need me until I stop. But the money talk with Greenvale would get tougher from 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the difference from the two-year one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years would be a fire in the hen house, but five years is a long winter we can plan for.

say: I'd call it a **fair warning** to use well.
I'd push the union for a **shared buying group**.
think: I'd be **stepping back** from the hens by 2034 anyway.
Five years gives **Ciarán** time to learn and decide.
do: Send Ciarán on **robot and AI courses**.
Hand over the hens to him **at 65**.
S3.quote: Two years would be a fire in the hen house, but five years is a long winter we can plan for.
fieldNote: The extra three years turn **panic** into a **plan**.
She makes it her **son's decision** rather than her own.

steps.text: Send her son on robot and AI courses as they appear

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2039. I'd be retired and Ciarán would be in his forties. That's his world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is plenty, and the farms that plan will be fine. I'd say it at the discussion group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm calm about this one. I'd hand over before anything big changes, and Ciarán would have years to choose. Bird flu would still be my bigger worry until I retire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hand the hens to Ciarán at 65 as planned. I'd let him lead on any AI tools in the meantime. And Declan and I would keep our savings safe for retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pleased for Ciarán, even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you hope for Ciarán?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I hope my son Ciarán buys a robot in 2039 and still walks the hen house every morning, because the hens will notice if he stops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything that would still trouble you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Greenvale, always. Packers get bigger, farms get smaller. That's been true my whole life, AI or not.

say: I'd say a **decade is plenty** for farms that plan ahead.
I'd say it at the **discussion group**, not anywhere louder.
think: I'd hand over to Ciarán **before anything big** changes.
**Bird flu** stays my bigger worry until I retire.
do: Let him **lead on AI** tools meanwhile.
feel: She feels **calm** and pleased for Ciarán.
S4.quote: I hope my son Ciarán buys a robot in 2039 and still walks the hen house every morning, because the hens will notice if he stops.
fieldNote: With robots in **2039**, the change lands on her **son**, not her.
Her lifelong worry about **packer power** outlasts AI.
She wants Ciarán to keep the **daily walk** through the hens.

steps.text: Hand the hens to her son at 65

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because robotic egg units would undercut us and Ciarán's future would go with the hens. What would help is fair contract rules for the packers and grants that help family farms buy the robots, not just the giants.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the birds. A robot will count eggs better than I do, but I can walk into a hen house and know in ten seconds that something's wrong.

headlineQuote: A robot will count eggs better than I do, but I can walk into a hen house and know in ten seconds that something's wrong.
portrait: Fatima is a **58-year-old co-owner** of Hillcrest, running 12,000 laying hens beside her husband's arable.
She uses **AI now and then**, adopting tools after neighbours prove them.
She carries **standing worries** about bird flu and the packer Greenvale's contract.
AGI by 2028 makes her **anxious** that robotic egg units halve her income.
With longer warning, she lets her son **Ciarán** lead the switch.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because robotic egg units would **undercut** Hillcrest.
whatWouldHelp: **Fair contract rules** for packers, and grants for family farms to buy robots.
